The Latticed sandperch Parapercis clathrata is a relatively small-bodied benthic predator common on sandy reef flats and lagoons across the Indo-Pacific. Field surveys indicate that adult females attain a maximum total length of approximately 24 cm [Li = approximately 24 cm], a size that is consistent among individuals from populations in the Philippines and the Great Barrier Reef. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows a power function derived from extensive specimen collections, and the estimated asymptotic wet weight for adult females is 116 grams [Wwi = 116 grams]. This ultimate body mass represents a plateau that individuals approach after several years of growth, a pattern typical of many serranid and pseudochromid fishes that inhabit structurally complex reef environments. Sexual size dimorphism is not pronounced in this species, though gravid females often appear slightly heavier due to ovarian development.

Recruitment into the adult population is contingent upon the completion of a pelagic larval phase and successful settlement onto suitable benthic substrates. In laboratory rearing experiments conducted at a stable water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the lifespan of Parapercis clathrata has been documented at approximately 2,920 days [am = approximately 2,920 days]. This longevity, exceeding eight years, is relatively extended for a teleost of this maximum length and likely reflects the low natural mortality rates afforded by its cryptic, crevice-dwelling lifestyle. Growth increments slow markedly after the first two years, with individuals approaching the asymptotic length well before mid-life. The longevity estimate is an important parameter for assessing population turnover rates and the resilience of this species to fishing pressure in its shallow-water habitats.

Reproductive maturity in the Latticed sandperch is attained at a modest body size, with individuals first becoming capable of spawning when they reach a total length of 11 cm [Lp = 11 cm]. The corresponding body mass at the onset of puberty is 10.6 grams [Wwp = 10.6 grams], a threshold that is typically reached during the second year of life under optimal thermal conditions. Females are batch spawners and exhibit a protracted reproductive season. When maintained at a water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], gravid females release clutches containing a mean of 71 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 71 eggs per spawning event], and the interval between successive spawning events averages approximately one event per day [F_R_i = approximately one event per day]. This rapid reproductive cycling allows individuals to produce a substantial total number of offspring over a single season, provided that food resources remain abundant.

The early life stages of Parapercis clathrata begin with the release of small, pelagic eggs that undergo external fertilisation during spawning events. Each fertilised ovum measures approximately 0.9 mm in diameter, and the calculated wet weight of a newly emerged larva at the moment of eclosion is 0.00038 grams [Wwb = 0.00038 grams]. This minuscule birth mass reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the endotrophic larva before it must initiate exogenous feeding. The transition to first feeding is a critical bottleneck; larvae that fail to encounter suitable planktonic prey within the first few days after mouth opening experience high mortality rates. The small egg size is characteristic of many tropical marine teleosts that produce numerous, relatively unprotected offspring as part of a high-fecundity, low-survivorship life-history strategy.

Comparative physiological studies conducted under controlled thermal regimes provide further context for the life-history traits of this species. At 28 °C [T = 28 °C], a temperature that approximates the mean annual conditions experienced by populations in the central Philippines, the daily reproductive output of Parapercis clathrata has been quantified in captive breeding experiments. The maximum reproductive rate, expressed as the product of clutch size and spawning frequency, amounts to approximately 71 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 71 eggs per day]. The high metabolic rates at this temperature support both rapid somatic growth and sustained gametogenesis, though they also impose substantial energetic demands that may limit longevity under resource-limited conditions. The combination of a moderate lifespan, early maturation at a small size, and continuous batch spawning enables this species to persist in dynamic reef environments where predation pressure on early life stages is intense.
